headline: Names under a wildcard registry get their own organizational domain, and the HTTP, DMARC and UUID citations name the specifications currently in force
summary:
`b.publicSuffix` ranked a matching exact rule above a matching wildcard rule. The Public Suffix List ranks by label count instead, so `x.kawasaki.jp` takes `*.kawasaki.jp` and not `jp` — and under the old order every name in such a registry collapsed onto the registry's own organizational domain. 275 of the list's 283 wildcard rules resolved that way. Anything deriving a boundary from that answer inherited it: DMARC relaxed alignment, cookie scope, same-site decisions. If you serve or accept mail from names under a wildcard registry, this changes what counts as aligned.

The rest of the release is the second half of a documentation-accuracy pass, where no behavior changes. What changes is that a reader checking the code against a specification is sent to a document that still exists in its own right.

The HTTP/1.1 series was replaced in 2022 by RFC 9110, 9111 and 9112, and the content was reorganized rather than renumbered — the section that defined a rule under RFC 7231 is generally not the same section number under RFC 9110. DMARC was replaced in the same way, and split three ways. UUIDs moved from RFC 4122 to RFC 9562. Roughly two hundred citations across the framework still pointed at the superseded documents.

Every replacement here was read off the successor's own table of contents rather than inferred, because inference is unreliable at this: 206 Partial Content did not stay in the range-requests section, and the DMARC rule for a message carrying two `From` headers moved from §6.6.1 to §5.3.1. Citations that are correct precisely because they name the older document — a parser that accepts vCard 3.0, a character set RFC 8187 dropped, a DMARC tag its successor removed — were identified and left alone.

If you have been reading a section number out of a blamejs comment and opening the RFC beside it, those numbers now resolve.

items.title: b.publicSuffix ranks a wildcard rule by its length, not below every exact rule
items.body:
The Public Suffix List algorithm picks the matching rule with the most labels, after exception rules, which outrank everything. This implementation instead placed every exact rule above every wildcard rule, so a one-label TLD beat a three-label wildcard beneath it. `x.kawasaki.jp` resolved to a public suffix of `jp` rather than to itself.

The effect is on the organizational domain, which is what `b.publicSuffix.organizationalDomain` returns and what several callers build a boundary from. Under the old order two unrelated names in the same wildcard registry both resolved to the registry's own domain, so `b.guardEnvelope` and `b.mailAuth` treated them as one organization for DMARC relaxed alignment, and anything scoping a cookie by organizational domain scoped it across the whole registry. 275 of the list's 283 wildcard rules sit beneath a listed TLD and were affected, among them `*.compute.amazonaws.com.cn`, `*.sch.uk` and the Japanese city registries.

An exact rule longer than a matching wildcard still wins, and an exception rule still outranks both. The published conformance suite that ships with the list now runs against the module on every test run, alongside the hand-written cases; it covers the wildcard registries directly, where the previous set exercised only `*.ck` — one of the eight wildcards no shorter rule can outrank, and so the one case that passes under either ordering.

If you derive trust or scope from an organizational domain and your names live under a wildcard registry, re-check anything you had pinned to the old answer.

items.title: The vendored Public Suffix List is current
items.body: Refreshed to the 2026-08-17 snapshot. Among the changes: `*.aivencloud.com`, `*.cursorusercontent.com`, `codepen.app`, `codepen.dev`, `here.now`, `online-server.cloud` and the Scaleway regional entries are now public suffixes, and `adaptable.app` no longer is.

items.title: HTTP citations name RFC 9110, 9111 and 9112
items.body:
RFC 7230 through 7235 were obsoleted in June 2022. Around eighty citations across twenty-five files still named them, in comments, in operator-facing error messages, and in the module blocks that generate the reference documentation.

The mapping is not arithmetic — the six documents were reorganized into three along different lines — so each section was confirmed against the successor's table of contents. A few that a reader might expect to have stayed put did not: 206 Partial Content is RFC 9110 §15.3.7 rather than anything under range requests, the authentication challenge grammar is §11.3, and establishing a protection space is §11.5. Cache-Control genuinely does keep §5.2, in RFC 9111.

No obsoleted HTTP-core citation remains in the framework's own source. Seven remain inside the vendored `@blamejs/pki` bundle, which ships in the package but is not edited here — those move when the bundle is next refreshed from upstream.

items.title: DMARC citations name RFC 9989, and the reporting ones name RFC 9990 or 9991
items.body:
RFC 7489 was replaced by three documents: the mechanism (RFC 9989), aggregate reporting (RFC 9990) and failure reporting (RFC 9991). Seventy-two citations moved, including the rule that decides what to do with a message carrying more than one `From` header — the header-duplication spoofing shape — which moved from §6.6.1 to §5.3.1.

The aggregate report XML schema is now RFC 9990 Appendix A and the email transport for those reports is §3.5.2, so `b.mail` cites those rather than RFC 7489's Appendix C.

One set of citations deliberately stays on RFC 7489. The `pct=` tag, which lets a domain apply its policy to a sample of failing mail, was removed in RFC 9989. `b.mailAuth` still honours it, because domains published `pct=` for a decade and those records are still in DNS: ignoring the tag would silently promote `p=reject; pct=10` from rejecting a tenth of failing mail to rejecting all of it. Dropping support is a deliverability decision to schedule, not a side effect of updating a reference, and the comments now say so.

items.title: UUID citations name RFC 9562
items.body:
RFC 4122 was obsoleted in May 2024. `b.uuid`, `b.guardUuid`, `b.safeSchema` and the request-identifier paths cite RFC 9562 now — §4 for the field layout, §4.1 for the variant field, §5.4 for version 4.

Worth noting for anyone who has written the same comment: RFC 9562 does not describe the `10xx` variant as "the RFC 4122 variant". It calls it the variant specified in that document, so the older phrasing was a stale reference rather than a name.

items.title: Three references named an unrelated document
items.body:
Reported from a downstream tree that vendors this package and swept it for the same class (#593). Each of these named a real RFC that is about something else entirely, so a reader who followed the number landed somewhere with no connection to the code beside it.

**Clear-Site-Data is not RFC 9527.** RFC 9527 specifies DHCPv6 options for the Homenet Naming Authority. Clear-Site-Data has no RFC at all — it is a W3C Working Draft, and the header field it defines is §3.1 there. The wrong number appeared eleven times including in the `@card` annotation that generates the reference page for `b.middleware.clearSiteData`, and in `b.session.logout`, which composes it.

**ML-DSA is RFC 9881, not RFC 9909.** RFC 9909 carries the SLH-DSA algorithm identifiers. The two were transposed in `b.cms`, in both directions, so ML-DSA cited the SLH-DSA document and SLH-DSA cited the ML-DSA one. The parameter-set subsections cited alongside them do not exist either: RFC 9881 defines all three ML-DSA OIDs in §2 and has no per-parameter-set section.

**BIMI is not RFC 9091.** RFC 9091 is the experimental DMARC extension for public suffix domains, which is itself now obsoleted. BIMI has never been published as an RFC — it is `draft-blank-ietf-bimi` — so `b.mail.bimi` cites the draft, including in its own module documentation. The header comment inside the vendored trust-anchor bundle still carries the old number: that file is verified against a recorded hash and is refreshed from upstream rather than edited here.

Also corrected: `b.jsonapi` described its `sort` direction as following the JSON specification, which says nothing about sort order.

items.title: Smaller corrections, and the citations left deliberately alone
items.body:
XMLDSig algorithm URIs are registered in RFC 6931; `PKIFailureInfo` bit names come from RFC 4210; the `filename*` encoding `b.static` emits is RFC 8187 §3.2.1.

Several references that a currency check flags are correct as they stand, and were kept: `b.safeVcard` cites RFC 2425 and 2426 for the vCard 3.0 shape it still accepts while naming RFC 6350 as its primary specification; `b.middleware.bodyParser` cites RFC 5987 for `iso-8859-1` because RFC 8187 removed that character set; and the S/MIME, 8BITMIME and PKCS #1 references already named both the current document and its predecessor.

items.title: The regex-literal scanner decides operand position by the closed rule
items.body:
The gate that keeps `b.guard*` and `b.safe*` free of regular expressions decided whether a `/` opened a literal by listing what may precede one. That list is open-ended, so every missing entry was a silent hole — and `return /unsafe/.test(value)`, the most natural way to write a guard predicate, sat in one (#589).

It now asks the closed question instead: does the previous token END an expression? An identifier, a literal, a closing bracket, or one of `this` / `super` / `true` / `false` / `null` does; every other reserved word leaves operand position, so a `/` after it opens a literal. That covers every keyword without naming one, which is the property the previous formulation lacked.

Re-scanning all seventy-eight files found nothing had slipped through the old rule, so the family really was clean; the gate simply could not have held it. The scanner now also runs a fixture table against itself on every execution — keyword positions, division and in-string controls, member names, and the contextual cases — because the original controls passed throughout the period the hole existed, which is why review did not catch it.

One bias is deliberate: `await` and `yield` are read as keywords even where they could be identifiers, so a file that names a variable `await` and divides by it needs an allow-marker. For a gate whose purpose is finding literals, over-detection costs a one-line marker and under-detection costs silence.

items.title: Three detector classes registered in the allow-marker table
items.body: `regex-in-guard-or-safe-primitive`, `release-script-capture-status-unchecked` and `sfv-citation-must-match-referencing-protocol` all offer the `// allow:<class>` escape hatch but were absent from the table that validates those markers, so a marker naming one of them would have been rejected as naming no detector (#594). Latent rather than breaking, because the marker scan and those detectors do not currently cover the same files — but it bites the moment either widens.
